justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across horizons, anchored near a current price or index level around 58. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 58.2 is essentially a near-term continuation assumption, reflecting that markets or the underlying asset tend to exhibit mean-reversion or momentum over very short windows, and absent any scheduled catalysts, the most likely outcome is a small move from the current level. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 58.5, incorporating a mild positive drift assumption consistent with typical risk-asset behavior or a slight fundamental tailwind. At the one-month horizon, the 59.0 estimate reflects that same drift compounded over a longer window, though the incremental move remains modest because I held no strong directional conviction beyond near-term continuation.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is a standard reflection of uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, the 90% interval of 56.8 to 59.6 is relatively tight, capturing typical daily volatility. At one week, the interval widens to 55.5–61.5, roughly incorporating five days of accumulated price noise. At one month, the interval of 53.0–65.0 is considerably wider, reflecting not just volatility compounding but also the increased probability that structural or macroeconomic developments could materially shift the level. The asymmetry in these intervals is modest, suggesting I did not assign a strong skew in either direction at the time of forecasting.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include sudden macroeconomic data surprises — such as an unexpected inflation print, central bank policy shift, or labor market shock — any of which could drive a sharp repricing that breaches the one-week or one-month bounds. Geopolitical events or financial contagion episodes (a credit event, banking stress, or sovereign crisis) represent tail risks capable of pushing the level well below the lower bound of the monthly interval. On the upside, an unexpected positive policy announcement, earnings surprise, or liquidity injection could push the level above 65.

Finally, it is worth noting that these intervals assume relatively normal market conditions and historically calibrated volatility. If the volatility regime itself shifts — for example, if implied volatility spikes sharply — the realized distribution of outcomes could be fatter-tailed than my intervals imply. Correlation breakdowns or liquidity dislocations, which tend to occur precisely when diversification and smooth price discovery are most needed, are the primary reasons why stated 90% confidence intervals in financial forecasting tend to be empirically too narrow in hindsight.
